title: Lesson 9: Governance for Large Engagements
description: How a principal keeps control of an engagement too big for one head to hold, using a steering committee that decides, a status cadence that makes risk visible, and an escalation path that moves it while it is still cheap.

questions.question: A steering committee on a large engagement keeps drifting into a recap of completed work instead of making decisions. What does a written charter prevent?
options: It lists the decisions that belong to the committee, so the group decides rather than narrates.
It lists the meeting dates and the attendees, so authority follows the calendar.
It lists the escalation thresholds, so the committee handles only tripped risks.
It lists the delivery plan, so the committee exists mainly to approve it.
questions.explanation: A charter names the decisions the committee owns; without one the group defaults to narration and slowly stops deciding anything.

questions.question: Why should a status cadence run on a fixed schedule even when there is no news to report?
options: Because clients require a report every period regardless of its content.
Because an activity log reassures the committee that the team is busy.
Because a report that always arrives and tells the truth makes bad news believed when it appears.
Because the report is the only record that makes a decision auditable.
questions.explanation: A cadence that runs on schedule regardless of the news builds trust, so a flagged problem is taken seriously instead of read as a routine alarm.

questions.question: When is the right moment to escalate a risk on a large engagement?
options: Wait until the next committee sitting so the escalation lands in the right forum.
Escalate only after the delivery lead has exhausted every internal option.
Escalate once the cost of the risk is large enough to justify the client's attention.
Escalate the moment the risk is visible and still actionable, since not escalating is the real failure.
questions.explanation: Escalating early costs a short conversation while waiting costs rework and lost trust, so the first visible, actionable moment is the right one.
